pedagogy.summary: Before a child can measure anything they must first SEE the attribute — length, height, weight, capacity — as something separable from an undifferentiated sense of 'big'. Young children typically call one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, taller, heavier, or holds more (CCSS Progression). The teaching work is to help the attribute 'stand out': to name several measurable attributes of a SINGLE object (a bottle has height AND weight AND capacity), to treat each as a different question, and to move from absolute labels ('I'm tall') to comparative relations ('taller than'). This differentiation is the conceptual root of the whole Measurement domain.
bestPractices: Talk through HOW you are comparing — 'this one is taller (more length up), that one has a bigger bottom (more area)' — so children learn to discriminate, name and label distinct attributes rather than saying 'bigger'

Take ONE object and hunt for all its measurable attributes: 'What could we measure about this bottle? Its height... what else? How heavy... what else? How much it holds' — building the idea that one object carries several attributes
Deliberately pit attributes against each other (a tall thin bottle vs a short wide jar) so the child cannot answer with a single global 'bigger' — they must pick the attribute
Move children from absolute descriptors ('tall', 'heavy') to comparative, gradational language ('taller than', 'the heaviest of these three') through many side-by-side comparisons
Use counterexamples that break false attribute links: a big beach ball is lighter than a small stone (big ≠ heavy); a tall glass need not hold more than a wide bowl (tall ≠ more)
Introduce measurement words as answers to specific questions ('how long?', 'how heavy?', 'how much?') so each attribute has its own question and its own comparative vocabulary
keyRepresentations: One object shown with three separate 'measuring lenses' — a length lens, a weight lens (balance), a capacity lens (fill) — each answering a different question about the same object
Two contrasting objects (tall+thin vs short+wide) where the winner changes depending on which attribute is chosen
Comparative word banks paired to each attribute: long/short, tall/short, heavy/light, full/empty, more/less
A balance scale and a pouring/filling demonstration to make weight and capacity felt as attributes distinct from how big something looks
commonMisconceptions: Undifferentiated 'bigger': treats length, height, area, weight and capacity as one global size, so the 'biggest-looking' object is assumed to be the longest AND heaviest AND to hold the most
Height–capacity conflation: a taller container is assumed to hold more, regardless of width
Size–weight conflation: a bigger object is assumed to be heavier
Absolute rather than comparative use of attribute words: labels each object 'tall' or 'big' but cannot say one is taller than another (treats 'tall' as a category, not a relation)
Recognises only a single attribute of an object ('how big it is') rather than seeing that one object has several measurable attributes

learn.summary: Help 4–6 year olds see that a single object has several separate measurable attributes — length/height, weight, and capacity — rather than one global sense of 'big'. The core work is differentiating each attribute, naming it, pairing it with its own question ('how long?', 'how heavy?', 'how much?'), and moving from absolute labels ('tall') to comparative relations ('taller than'). The strongest insight comes from comparing the SAME two contrasting objects (tall-thin vs short-wide) where which one wins changes depending on which attribute you apply.

activities.title: Measuring lenses: watch which one wins change
feedback: If the wider jar takes all the water with room to spare, narrate: 'This one is taller, but this one holds more — those are different things to measure.' If they hold about the same, say so: 'Taller did not mean it holds more.'
If the child says one object is just 'bigger', ask 'bigger in which way — taller, heavier, or holds more?' and let them test each.
Announce each result with its comparative word: 'taller', 'heavier', 'holds more'.
activities.rationale: Differentiating attributes is felt when the same objects win on different attributes depending on which one is applied. An interactive model where the child drags a length, weight, and capacity 'lens' onto each object and sees the comparison change makes this concrete; a live label announcing the attribute and comparative word makes the mechanism explicit. These are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms — the same comparison can be staged with a real ruler, balance, and jug of water.
sourceClaims: Kindergarteners hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling an object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; the attribute must be discriminated from an undifferentiated sense of amount before it can be measured. Students should learn to distinguish, label and describe several measurable attributes of a single object (K.MD.1). Length is the distance between the endpoints of an object.

KS1 pupils should compare, describe and solve practical problems for lengths/heights, mass/weight and capacity/volume using comparative vocabulary (long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short, heavy/light, full/empty, more/less).
learnerActions: Place a tall thin bottle and a short wide jar side by side.
Apply a length comparison (e.g. a ruler lens or measuring them against each other): name the taller as the winner — 'taller'.
Apply a weight comparison (e.g. a balance that tips to the heavier): name which is heavier.

Apply a capacity comparison: fill the tall bottle to the top and pour it into the wide jar; if the jar takes it all with room to spare it holds more. Choose containers where the pour really shows this, and let the actual result stand.
Say aloud which object wins for each attribute, using the matching comparative word.
Notice that the same two objects can win on different attributes, so there is no single answer to 'which is bigger?'
activities.intendedInsight: There is no single 'bigger': each object has a height, a weight, and a capacity, and these are different questions with different answers. When which object wins changes per attribute, 'bigger' dissolves into separate, nameable attributes.

activities.title: One object, many attributes — collect the tags
feedback: After each tag: 'Good — that's one thing. What else could we measure about the very same object?'
If the child stops at one attribute, prompt the regions: 'How tall... how heavy... how much it holds?'
activities.rationale: Taking one object and hunting for all its attributes directly builds the one-object-many-attributes idea. A tap-to-reveal interactive image (tap the side → 'height', the base → 'how heavy', the inside → 'how much it holds') can scaffold this, as can simply handling a real bottle. Tap-to-reveal shows each attribute but does not dynamically change which object wins a comparison, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: Kindergarteners hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling an object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; the attribute must be discriminated from an undifferentiated sense of amount before it can be measured. Students should learn to distinguish, label and describe several measurable attributes of a single object (K.MD.1). Length is the distance between the endpoints of an object.
learnerActions: Take a single object (e.g. a bottle) and ask: 'What could we measure about this?'
Find its height (point to or measure the side), collect a 'height' tag.
Find how heavy it is (hold it or place it on a balance), collect a 'weight' tag.
Find how much it holds (fill it), collect a 'capacity' tag.
Repeat 'what else can we measure?' until height, weight and capacity have all been named for the one object, and welcome any others the child suggests (such as how wide it is).
activities.intendedInsight: One object carries several measurable attributes at once; recognising only 'how big it is' misses the others.

activities.title: Counterexamples that break false links
feedback: When the small stone outweighs the big ball: 'Small to look at, but heavier to hold — size and weight are different attributes.'
If the child insists the bigger one must be heavier, let them feel both and narrate the surprise.
activities.rationale: Counterexamples that break false attribute links (big ≠ heavy, tall ≠ more) directly address the size–weight and height–capacity conflations that are central misconceptions here. A balance and a pouring demonstration make weight and capacity felt as attributes distinct from visual size. Choose objects that reliably produce the intended contrast and confirm by weighing or pouring.
sourceClaims: Kindergarteners hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling an object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; the attribute must be discriminated from an undifferentiated sense of amount before it can be measured. Students should learn to distinguish, label and describe several measurable attributes of a single object (K.MD.1). Length is the distance between the endpoints of an object.
learnerActions: Compare a big beach ball and a small stone: predict which is heavier, then check by holding each or on a balance.
If you chose a dense stone that really is heavier than the ball (check this beforehand), the child finds the small stone is heavier — big does not always mean heavy.

Compare a tall glass and a wide bowl (chosen in advance so that the bowl really holds more): predict which holds more, then fill and pour to check, and let the actual result stand — tall does not always mean holds more.
State the lesson: 'The bigger or taller one is not always the heavier one, or the one that holds more.'
activities.intendedInsight: Attributes are different things to measure and do not always go together: something can be tall but light, or big but hold less. You cannot reliably tell one attribute just by looking at another — you have to check.

activities.title: From 'tall' to 'taller than' — comparative language
feedback: If the child says 'they're both tall', invite ordering: 'Yes — and which of these two is TALLER?'
Do not mark absolute-language answers wrong; keep offering graded pairs so comparative language emerges with experience.
activities.rationale: Moving children from absolute descriptors to comparative, gradational language through many side-by-side comparisons is a documented instructional focus at this level; absolute-to-comparative use tends to resolve with experience rather than drilling.
sourceClaims: At the Length Quantity Recognizer level a child identifies length/distance as an attribute but may understand it as an absolute descriptor (e.g. all adults are 'tall') rather than a comparative (one person is taller than another); instruction focuses on differentiating length from other measures of size such as area or volume and moving children past simple tall/short classifications to gradations and relationships.

KS1 pupils should compare, describe and solve practical problems for lengths/heights, mass/weight and capacity/volume using comparative vocabulary (long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short, heavy/light, full/empty, more/less).
learnerActions: Given a ribbon described as 'long', ask: 'Longer than what?' Find something it is longer than and something it is shorter than.
Order three objects by one attribute: 'Which is the tallest of these three? Which is the shortest?'
Describe pairs using comparative words: longer/shorter, taller/shorter, heavier/lighter, fuller/emptier, more/less.
Practise across many side-by-side pairs so relations, not fixed categories, become the habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Attribute words name relations between objects, not fixed boxes. 'Tall' invites the question 'taller than what?'

activities.title: Sort words and questions to their attribute
feedback: If the child picks the taller option for 'holds more', ask 'is that about how tall, or how much it holds?' and prompt a fill-to-check.
Confirm correct sorts by restating the pairing: 'heavy tells us about weight.'
activities.rationale: Categorising words and questions by attribute can build clean discrimination and vocabulary and can check attribute-naming. This recognition-style sorting assesses and reinforces attribute names but does not, on its own, let the child observe which object wins change across attributes or construct language in a live comparison — combine it with the comparison and pouring activities.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should compare, describe and solve practical problems for lengths/heights, mass/weight and capacity/volume using comparative vocabulary (long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short, heavy/light, full/empty, more/less).
learnerActions: Sort attribute words to the thing they measure: long/short/tall → length or height; heavy/light → weight; holds more/holds less → capacity (full/empty describe how much is in a container compared with what it can hold).
For a question like 'which holds more?', name which attribute it asks about before answering.
Answer a 'which holds more?' question using containers checked in advance so that the taller-but-thinner one really holds less; justify by capacity, not height, and confirm by filling and pouring.
activities.intendedInsight: Each attribute has its own question and its own comparative words; identifying the attribute a question asks about comes before answering it.

constraints: Sorting/matching and multiple-choice ('which attribute does this word measure?') can assess and reinforce recognition of attribute names; they do not, by themselves, let the child observe which object wins change across attributes or construct attribute language in a live comparison — pair them with hands-on comparison and pouring.
Tap-to-reveal of an object's attributes shows one-object-many-attributes but does not dynamically change which object wins a comparison; use it alongside a comparison activity.

Absolute vs comparative language is developmental: provide many graded side-by-side comparisons and let comparative relations emerge; do not drill comparative vocabulary in isolation or mark absolute answers wrong.

Capacity outcomes depend on the actual containers: a wide jar holding more than a tall bottle must be verified by filling and pouring, not assumed, and must NOT be described as 'the one that overflows first holds more' (the first to overflow actually holds less). Choose containers where the pour genuinely demonstrates the point, and let the real result stand.

Counterexample outcomes (big ball lighter than small stone; tall glass vs wide bowl) depend on the specific objects chosen; pick objects that reliably produce the intended contrast and confirm by weighing or pouring rather than asserting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One legacy source (UK National Curriculum KS1) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim accordingly.

The original recommendation stated the 'WIDE jar overflows first — it holds more', which is internally inconsistent: the container that overflows first holds less. The capacity demonstration has been reframed as pouring the tall bottle into the wide jar and checking for room to spare; the actual outcome depends on the containers and must be checked with the materials.

The legacy entry included a 'conversation' approach rated 'poor' and a '3D' approach rated 'possible' with the claim that 3D 'adds cost without sharpening the core insight'; these comparative-efficacy and necessity judgements are catalog preferences, not established findings, and have been omitted or softened. Hands-on handling of real objects is used in the recommended activities to feel weight and capacity.

The claim that conversation 'cannot render' comparing real quantities is a catalog ranking, not an objective limit, and was not propagated; dialogue can still support naming and prompting during hands-on comparison.

The original pedagogy also mentions area as a measurable attribute; the objective and evidence name length/height/weight/capacity, so area appears only within the quoted source claim and is not built into a separate activity.

assess.poeTask: Stand the tall thin bottle and the short wide jar side by side. Ask the child to PREDICT which holds more water, and to say WHY, before anything is poured — the stated reason is the diagnostic part. Then fill the tall bottle to the top and pour it into the wide jar (and/or fill each from a jug). A child who conflates height with capacity predicts the tall bottle holds more; when the wide jar takes all the water with room to spare (or holds the same), the prediction is violated. Explain: how tall a container is does not tell you how much it holds — they are different attributes.
probeDeeper: 'Tell me one thing about this bottle we could measure. Now another. And one more.' (checks the child sees several attributes of one object)
Counterexample: 'Here is a big beach ball and a small stone. Which is heavier? Is the bigger one always the heavier one?' (separates size from weight)
'This ribbon is long. Longer than what? Show me something it is longer than, and something it is shorter than.' (moves absolute → comparative)
'Can something be tall but light? Can you point to one?' (tests that attributes vary independently)
assess.correctAnswer: No — you cannot tell just from height. How tall something is and how much it holds are different things to measure; the wide jar could hold the same or even more. To find out which holds more you would have to fill them and compare the amount, not just look at which is taller.

errorPatterns.pattern: Undifferentiated 'bigger': 'yes, A is taller so it is bigger, so it holds the most' — collapses height, size and capacity into one global quantity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pour to show a wide jar holding as much as or more than a taller bottle; narrate the attributes separately ('this one is taller, but this one holds more'); build the habit of naming which attribute a question asks about before answering.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — A is taller, so it is bigger, so it holds the most water
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers yes and justifies by 'it's taller/bigger'; uses 'big' for every comparison; cannot separate the question 'how tall' from 'how much it holds'

errorPatterns.pattern: Absolute, not comparative: labels each object 'tall' or 'big' as a fixed category and cannot place them in a taller-than relation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill comparative vocabulary in isolation or mark it wrong — it resolves with experience. Provide many side-by-side comparisons of graded lengths so the child hears and uses 'taller than / shorter than' about real pairs, letting comparative relations emerge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'they're both tall' or 'it's tall' without ordering them; resists 'which is TALLER'; treats tall/short as boxes rather than a comparison

errorPatterns.pattern: Size–weight (or size–capacity) conflation on other attributes: assumes the bigger-looking object is automatically the heavier one
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance and counterexamples (small stone sinks the scale against a big light ball); separate 'how big it looks' from 'how heavy it is' as different measurable attributes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up (big beach ball vs small stone) says the big one is heavier; links appearance-of-size directly to weight

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'big/bigger' for everything; says the taller bottle holds more and is heavier; cannot name attributes separately or place objects in a comparative relation.
responseLevels.full: Names several measurable attributes of one object (a bottle has height, weight and capacity), treats them as separate questions, and reasons that being taller does not decide which holds more — you would fill or weigh to find out — using comparative language across a new pair unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can name one or two attributes and compare on the obvious one (which is taller), but still links them — assumes taller means holds more, or bigger means heavier — listing attributes without treating them as independent.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a tall, thin bottle (A) next to a short, wide jar (B). Say: 'A is taller than B. Does the taller one always hold the most water? Tell me yes or no — and then tell me how you decided.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has NOT differentiated the attributes answers from a single global size — 'yes, the taller one is bigger so it holds more'. A child who HAS differentiated says height does not decide capacity: they are separate attributes, and you would pour or fill to compare how much each holds. The two lines of reasoning give opposite answers, and answering 'no' for the right reason requires actually separating height from capacity.
